derby_ai_phd.proposal:
Prepared for: University of Derby – School of Computing, Data Science Research Centre

Fit with Derby: the Data Science Research Centre in the School of Computing works on machine learning and data science with industry links; the project would sit naturally there and I would welcome the supervisor's guidance on scope, ethics approval and any College-specific requirements.

Title
Calibrated, decision-aware uncertainty for machine learning in drilling and industrial asset monitoring under distribution shift

1. Background and motivation
Machine-learning models are increasingly used to support high-stakes engineering decisions: interpreting well logs while drilling, detecting abnormal operating states and scheduling maintenance of gas compressors and turbines. In these settings the cost of an unreliable prediction is large, yet the standard evaluation (random train/test splits and average accuracy) hides the failure that matters: a model that is well calibrated on average can be badly miscalibrated on a particular well, machine or operating regime. My professional work as a petroleum (drilling) engineer and as the developer of AI products for oil and gas, health and other industrial domains has repeatedly shown this gap between benchmark performance and decision-ready reliability.

Preliminary, unpublished experiments on public data illustrate the problem. In a well-log facies study on the FORCE 2020 data (81 wells), split conformal prediction reached an average coverage of 0.889 against a 0.90 target, but the worst well reached only 0.599 and 19 of 81 wells fell below 0.85. In an alarm-design study on real Petrobras 3W instances (1,119 events) the false-alarm rate was 0.147 against a target of 0.10. These are early results from prototypes, not validated findings; they motivate the question below.

2. Aims and research questions
Aim: to develop and rigorously evaluate uncertainty-quantification methods whose guarantees hold per well, per asset and under distribution shift, and that connect directly to operational decisions.
RQ1. How can group-conditional and adaptive conformal prediction, and Bayesian ensembles, be made reliable at the level of individual wells or machines when the test distribution differs from the training data?
RQ2. How should calibrated uncertainty be coupled to cost-sensitive decisions (alarm, referral to an expert, intervention) so that operational costs, not only accuracy, are minimised?
RQ3. Can domain structure (stratigraphic transition grammars, drilling mechanics, physics-based digital twins) improve validity and sample efficiency without sacrificing coverage?

3. Literature and positioning
The work builds on conformal prediction and its group-conditional, adaptive and shift-aware extensions, on Bayesian deep learning and deep ensembles, on cost-sensitive decision theory, and on physics-informed and structured prediction in geoscience and prognostics. The gap I address is empirical and methodological: few studies evaluate guarantees on a leave-one-well-out or leave-one-asset-out basis with real industrial benchmarks, and fewer connect the guarantees to decision costs. A full literature review will be completed in the first year.

4. Methodology
(a) Evaluation protocol: leave-one-well-out and leave-one-asset-out splits, worst-group coverage and decision-cost metrics reported alongside averages. (b) Methods: group-conditional and adaptive conformal prediction, Bayesian deep ensembles, structured decoding with domain grammars, and cost-sensitive referral policies; reinforcement learning for sequential decisions will be considered where a simulator exists. (c) Data: public datasets only (FORCE 2020 and SEG 2016 well logs, Petrobras 3W v2, NASA IMS bearings, further sets identified in year one), with licences verified before use; industrial data would be used only under a confidentiality agreement. (d) Software: an open-source, tested and reproducible toolkit.

5. Work plan (three years)
Year 1: literature review; reproducible baselines and the evaluation protocol; first paper on per-well coverage failure and remedies.
Year 2: decision-aware calibration and structured decoding; second paper; secondment or collaboration with an industrial partner where possible.
Year 3: extension to prognostics and digital twins; third paper; thesis writing and open-source release.

6. Expected outcomes and impact
Three peer-reviewed papers, an open benchmark protocol and software toolkit, and guidance for deploying trustworthy ML in safety-critical industrial settings. Negative results will be reported openly.

7. Ethics, data and intellectual property
Only public data will be used unless an agreement is in place. Technical details of my existing patent applications are confidential and will not be disclosed or used without separate agreement.

8. Why me
MSc in Petroleum Engineering (Drilling) and several years of industrial and product-development experience, including digital-twin and predictive-maintenance work for gas compressors and turbines. English proficiency: C2.

Statement of purpose / motivation letter (draft)

Prepared for: University of Derby – School of Computing, Data Science Research Centre

Dear Admissions Committee,

I am a petroleum (drilling) engineer who builds AI products for oil and gas, health and other industrial domains. The question that has followed me through every project is simple: when can a model's prediction be trusted for a specific well, machine or patient? I am applying to University of Derby – School of Computing, Data Science Research Centre to turn this question into rigorous doctoral research on calibrated, decision-aware uncertainty for machine learning under distribution shift.

My training is an MSc in Petroleum Engineering (Drilling) and a BSc in Petroleum Engineering (Exploitation of Oil Resources). Since then I have led a knowledge-based start-up, Petro Pala Toos, and founded further technology start-ups, developing digital-twin and predictive-maintenance work for gas compressors and turbines and AI products in health. I have filed 37 patent applications in Iran across eight domains; they are currently under review by the Patent Office, and I can discuss technical details under a confidentiality agreement. My English proficiency is C2.

Preliminary, unpublished experiments on public data motivate this work. On 81 wells from the FORCE 2020 dataset, split conformal prediction reached an average coverage of 0.889 against a 0.90 target, yet the worst well reached only 0.599. These are early prototype results, not validated findings, but they show the gap between average and worst-case reliability that I want to study rigorously.

Why this programme: The Data Science Research Centre in the School of Computing works on machine learning and data science with industry links; the project would sit naturally there and I would welcome the supervisor's guidance on scope, ethics approval and any College-specific requirements.

During the PhD I plan to (1) develop methods that give well-level or machine-level reliability guarantees under distribution shift, (2) evaluate them on public benchmarks in drilling, condition monitoring and health data, and (3) release reproducible code. I am used to working with real, messy industrial data and delivering working systems, and I want to complement that with the methodological depth a doctoral programme provides.

I would welcome the chance to discuss the project with potential supervisors. Thank you for considering my application.

Sincerely,
Mohammad Parsa Sohrabi

ucl_dla.proposal:
Prepared for: UCL – Centre for Artificial Intelligence (EPSRC DLA)

Fit with UCL: the UCL Centre for Artificial Intelligence hosts statistical machine learning and foundational AI research; the project asks for reliable uncertainty with per-group guarantees on industrial data.

Title
Calibrated, decision-aware uncertainty for machine learning in drilling and industrial asset monitoring under distribution shift

1. Background and motivation
Machine-learning models are increasingly used to support high-stakes engineering decisions: interpreting well logs while drilling, detecting abnormal operating states and scheduling maintenance of gas compressors and turbines. In these settings the cost of an unreliable prediction is large, yet the standard evaluation (random train/test splits and average accuracy) hides the failure that matters: a model that is well calibrated on average can be badly miscalibrated on a particular well, machine or operating regime. My professional work as a petroleum (drilling) engineer and as the developer of AI products for oil and gas, health and other industrial domains has repeatedly shown this gap between benchmark performance and decision-ready reliability.

Preliminary, unpublished experiments on public data illustrate the problem. In a well-log facies study on the FORCE 2020 data (81 wells), split conformal prediction reached an average coverage of 0.889 against a 0.90 target, but the worst well reached only 0.599 and 19 of 81 wells fell below 0.85. In an alarm-design study on real Petrobras 3W instances (1,119 events) the false-alarm rate was 0.147 against a target of 0.10. These are early results from prototypes, not validated findings; they motivate the question below.

2. Aims and research questions
Aim: to develop and rigorously evaluate uncertainty-quantification methods whose guarantees hold per well, per asset and under distribution shift, and that connect directly to operational decisions.
RQ1. How can group-conditional and adaptive conformal prediction, and Bayesian ensembles, be made reliable at the level of individual wells or machines when the test distribution differs from the training data?
RQ2. How should calibrated uncertainty be coupled to cost-sensitive decisions (alarm, referral to an expert, intervention) so that operational costs, not only accuracy, are minimised?
RQ3. Can domain structure (stratigraphic transition grammars, drilling mechanics, physics-based digital twins) improve validity and sample efficiency without sacrificing coverage?

3. Literature and positioning
The work builds on conformal prediction and its group-conditional, adaptive and shift-aware extensions, on Bayesian deep learning and deep ensembles, on cost-sensitive decision theory, and on physics-informed and structured prediction in geoscience and prognostics. The gap I address is empirical and methodological: few studies evaluate guarantees on a leave-one-well-out or leave-one-asset-out basis with real industrial benchmarks, and fewer connect the guarantees to decision costs. A full literature review will be completed in the first year.

4. Methodology
(a) Evaluation protocol: leave-one-well-out and leave-one-asset-out splits, worst-group coverage and decision-cost metrics reported alongside averages. (b) Methods: group-conditional and adaptive conformal prediction, Bayesian deep ensembles, structured decoding with domain grammars, and cost-sensitive referral policies; reinforcement learning for sequential decisions will be considered where a simulator exists. (c) Data: public datasets only (FORCE 2020 and SEG 2016 well logs, Petrobras 3W v2, NASA IMS bearings, further sets identified in year one), with licences verified before use; industrial data would be used only under a confidentiality agreement. (d) Software: an open-source, tested and reproducible toolkit.

5. Work plan (three years)
Year 1: literature review; reproducible baselines and the evaluation protocol; first paper on per-well coverage failure and remedies.
Year 2: decision-aware calibration and structured decoding; second paper; secondment or collaboration with an industrial partner where possible.
Year 3: extension to prognostics and digital twins; third paper; thesis writing and open-source release.

6. Expected outcomes and impact
Three peer-reviewed papers, an open benchmark protocol and software toolkit, and guidance for deploying trustworthy ML in safety-critical industrial settings. Negative results will be reported openly.

7. Ethics, data and intellectual property
Only public data will be used unless an agreement is in place. Technical details of my existing patent applications are confidential and will not be disclosed or used without separate agreement.

8. Why me
MSc in Petroleum Engineering (Drilling) and several years of industrial and product-development experience, including digital-twin and predictive-maintenance work for gas compressors and turbines. English proficiency: C2.

vector_gsp.proposal:
Prepared for: Vector Institute – Ontario / British Columbia (Toronto, UBC)

Fit with Vector: the Vector Institute's faculty work on trustworthy machine learning and uncertainty quantification; the project targets reliability of machine-learning decisions in industrial settings.

Title
Calibrated, decision-aware uncertainty for machine learning in drilling and industrial asset monitoring under distribution shift

1. Background and motivation
Machine-learning models are increasingly used to support high-stakes engineering decisions: interpreting well logs while drilling, detecting abnormal operating states and scheduling maintenance of gas compressors and turbines. In these settings the cost of an unreliable prediction is large, yet the standard evaluation (random train/test splits and average accuracy) hides the failure that matters: a model that is well calibrated on average can be badly miscalibrated on a particular well, machine or operating regime. My professional work as a petroleum (drilling) engineer and as the developer of AI products for oil and gas, health and other industrial domains has repeatedly shown this gap between benchmark performance and decision-ready reliability.

Preliminary, unpublished experiments on public data illustrate the problem. In a well-log facies study on the FORCE 2020 data (81 wells), split conformal prediction reached an average coverage of 0.889 against a 0.90 target, but the worst well reached only 0.599 and 19 of 81 wells fell below 0.85. In an alarm-design study on real Petrobras 3W instances (1,119 events) the false-alarm rate was 0.147 against a target of 0.10. These are early results from prototypes, not validated findings; they motivate the question below.

2. Aims and research questions
Aim: to develop and rigorously evaluate uncertainty-quantification methods whose guarantees hold per well, per asset and under distribution shift, and that connect directly to operational decisions.
RQ1. How can group-conditional and adaptive conformal prediction, and Bayesian ensembles, be made reliable at the level of individual wells or machines when the test distribution differs from the training data?
RQ2. How should calibrated uncertainty be coupled to cost-sensitive decisions (alarm, referral to an expert, intervention) so that operational costs, not only accuracy, are minimised?
RQ3. Can domain structure (stratigraphic transition grammars, drilling mechanics, physics-based digital twins) improve validity and sample efficiency without sacrificing coverage?

3. Literature and positioning
The work builds on conformal prediction and its group-conditional, adaptive and shift-aware extensions, on Bayesian deep learning and deep ensembles, on cost-sensitive decision theory, and on physics-informed and structured prediction in geoscience and prognostics. The gap I address is empirical and methodological: few studies evaluate guarantees on a leave-one-well-out or leave-one-asset-out basis with real industrial benchmarks, and fewer connect the guarantees to decision costs. A full literature review will be completed in the first year.

4. Methodology
(a) Evaluation protocol: leave-one-well-out and leave-one-asset-out splits, worst-group coverage and decision-cost metrics reported alongside averages. (b) Methods: group-conditional and adaptive conformal prediction, Bayesian deep ensembles, structured decoding with domain grammars, and cost-sensitive referral policies; reinforcement learning for sequential decisions will be considered where a simulator exists. (c) Data: public datasets only (FORCE 2020 and SEG 2016 well logs, Petrobras 3W v2, NASA IMS bearings, further sets identified in year one), with licences verified before use; industrial data would be used only under a confidentiality agreement. (d) Software: an open-source, tested and reproducible toolkit.

5. Work plan (three years)
Year 1: literature review; reproducible baselines and the evaluation protocol; first paper on per-well coverage failure and remedies.
Year 2: decision-aware calibration and structured decoding; second paper; secondment or collaboration with an industrial partner where possible.
Year 3: extension to prognostics and digital twins; third paper; thesis writing and open-source release.

6. Expected outcomes and impact
Three peer-reviewed papers, an open benchmark protocol and software toolkit, and guidance for deploying trustworthy ML in safety-critical industrial settings. Negative results will be reported openly.

7. Ethics, data and intellectual property
Only public data will be used unless an agreement is in place. Technical details of my existing patent applications are confidential and will not be disclosed or used without separate agreement.

8. Why me
MSc in Petroleum Engineering (Drilling) and several years of industrial and product-development experience, including digital-twin and predictive-maintenance work for gas compressors and turbines. English proficiency: C2.

Statement of purpose / motivation letter (draft)

Prepared for: Vector Institute – Ontario / British Columbia (Toronto, UBC)

Dear Admissions Committee,

I am a petroleum (drilling) engineer who builds AI products for oil and gas, health and other industrial domains. The question that has followed me through every project is simple: when can a model's prediction be trusted for a specific well, machine or patient? I am applying to Vector Institute – Ontario / British Columbia (Toronto, UBC) to turn this question into rigorous doctoral research on calibrated, decision-aware uncertainty for machine learning under distribution shift.

My training is an MSc in Petroleum Engineering (Drilling) and a BSc in Petroleum Engineering (Exploitation of Oil Resources). Since then I have led a knowledge-based start-up, Petro Pala Toos, and founded further technology start-ups, developing digital-twin and predictive-maintenance work for gas compressors and turbines and AI products in health. I have filed 37 patent applications in Iran across eight domains; they are currently under review by the Patent Office, and I can discuss technical details under a confidentiality agreement. My English proficiency is C2.

Preliminary, unpublished experiments on public data motivate this work. On 81 wells from the FORCE 2020 dataset, split conformal prediction reached an average coverage of 0.889 against a 0.90 target, yet the worst well reached only 0.599. These are early prototype results, not validated findings, but they show the gap between average and worst-case reliability that I want to study rigorously.

Why this programme: The Vector Institute's faculty work on trustworthy machine learning and uncertainty quantification; the project targets reliability of machine-learning decisions in industrial settings.

During the PhD I plan to (1) develop methods that give well-level or machine-level reliability guarantees under distribution shift, (2) evaluate them on public benchmarks in drilling, condition monitoring and health data, and (3) release reproducible code. I am used to working with real, messy industrial data and delivering working systems, and I want to complement that with the methodological depth a doctoral programme provides.

I would welcome the chance to discuss the project with potential supervisors. Thank you for considering my application.

Sincerely,
Mohammad Parsa Sohrabi

Title

My professional work as a petroleum (drilling) engineer and as the developer of AI products for oil and gas, health and other industrial domains has repeatedly shown this gap between benchmark performance and decision-ready reliability.

In a well-log facies study on the FORCE 2020 data (81 wells), split conformal prediction reached an average coverage of 0.889 against a 0.90 target, but the worst well reached only 0.599 and 19 of 81 wells fell below 0.85. Aim: to develop and rigorously evaluate uncertainty-quantification methods whose guarantees hold per well, per asset and under distribution shift, and that connect directly to operational decisions.

Prepared for: Max Planck Institute for Informatics / Saarland (Computer Vision and Machine Learning)

Dear Admissions Committee,

I am a petroleum (drilling) engineer who builds AI products for oil and gas, health and other industrial domains. The question that has followed me through every project is simple: when can a model's prediction be trusted for a specific well, machine or patient? I am applying to Max Planck Institute for Informatics / Saarland (Computer Vision and Machine Learning) to turn this question into rigorous doctoral research on calibrated, decision-aware uncertainty for machine learning under distribution shift.

My training is an MSc in Petroleum Engineering (Drilling) and a BSc in Petroleum Engineering (Exploitation of Oil Resources). Since then I have led a knowledge-based start-up, Petro Pala Toos, and founded further technology start-ups, developing digital-twin and predictive-maintenance work for gas compressors and turbines and AI products in health. I have filed 37 patent applications in Iran across eight domains; they are currently under review by the Patent Office, and I can discuss technical details under a confidentiality agreement. My English proficiency is C2.

Preliminary, unpublished experiments on public data motivate this work. On 81 wells from the FORCE 2020 dataset, split conformal prediction reached an average coverage of 0.889 against a 0.90 target, yet the worst well reached only 0.599. These are early prototype results, not validated findings, but they show the gap between average and worst-case reliability that I want to study rigorously.

Why this programme: The Computer Vision and Machine Learning department works on machine learning that knows how much it knows; the project studies calibrated uncertainty with per-group guarantees.

During the PhD I plan to (1) develop methods that give well-level or machine-level reliability guarantees under distribution shift, (2) evaluate them on public benchmarks in drilling, condition monitoring and health data, and (3) release reproducible code. I am used to working with real, messy industrial data and delivering working systems, and I want to complement that with the methodological depth a doctoral programme provides.

I would welcome the chance to discuss the project with potential supervisors. Thank you for considering my application.

Sincerely,
Mohammad Parsa Sohrabi

dkfz_ds_health.proposal:
Prepared for: DKFZ Heidelberg – Data Science and Health / Medical Image Computing

Fit with DKFZ: groups on robust, uncertainty-aware machine learning for medical imaging and oncology; the project transfers calibrated-uncertainty methods from industrial data to clinical decision support.

Title
Calibrated, decision-aware uncertainty for machine learning in drilling and industrial asset monitoring under distribution shift

1. Background and motivation
Machine-learning models are increasingly used to support high-stakes engineering decisions: interpreting well logs while drilling, detecting abnormal operating states and scheduling maintenance of gas compressors and turbines. In these settings the cost of an unreliable prediction is large, yet the standard evaluation (random train/test splits and average accuracy) hides the failure that matters: a model that is well calibrated on average can be badly miscalibrated on a particular well, machine or operating regime. My professional work as a petroleum (drilling) engineer and as the developer of AI products for oil and gas, health and other industrial domains has repeatedly shown this gap between benchmark performance and decision-ready reliability.

Preliminary, unpublished experiments on public data illustrate the problem. In a well-log facies study on the FORCE 2020 data (81 wells), split conformal prediction reached an average coverage of 0.889 against a 0.90 target, but the worst well reached only 0.599 and 19 of 81 wells fell below 0.85. In an alarm-design study on real Petrobras 3W instances (1,119 events) the false-alarm rate was 0.147 against a target of 0.10. These are early results from prototypes, not validated findings; they motivate the question below.

2. Aims and research questions
Aim: to develop and rigorously evaluate uncertainty-quantification methods whose guarantees hold per well, per asset and under distribution shift, and that connect directly to operational decisions.
RQ1. How can group-conditional and adaptive conformal prediction, and Bayesian ensembles, be made reliable at the level of individual wells or machines when the test distribution differs from the training data?
RQ2. How should calibrated uncertainty be coupled to cost-sensitive decisions (alarm, referral to an expert, intervention) so that operational costs, not only accuracy, are minimised?
RQ3. Can domain structure (stratigraphic transition grammars, drilling mechanics, physics-based digital twins) improve validity and sample efficiency without sacrificing coverage?

3. Literature and positioning
The work builds on conformal prediction and its group-conditional, adaptive and shift-aware extensions, on Bayesian deep learning and deep ensembles, on cost-sensitive decision theory, and on physics-informed and structured prediction in geoscience and prognostics. The gap I address is empirical and methodological: few studies evaluate guarantees on a leave-one-well-out or leave-one-asset-out basis with real industrial benchmarks, and fewer connect the guarantees to decision costs. A full literature review will be completed in the first year.

4. Methodology
(a) Evaluation protocol: leave-one-well-out and leave-one-asset-out splits, worst-group coverage and decision-cost metrics reported alongside averages. (b) Methods: group-conditional and adaptive conformal prediction, Bayesian deep ensembles, structured decoding with domain grammars, and cost-sensitive referral policies; reinforcement learning for sequential decisions will be considered where a simulator exists. (c) Data: public datasets only (FORCE 2020 and SEG 2016 well logs, Petrobras 3W v2, NASA IMS bearings, further sets identified in year one), with licences verified before use; industrial data would be used only under a confidentiality agreement. (d) Software: an open-source, tested and reproducible toolkit.

5. Work plan (three years)
Year 1: literature review; reproducible baselines and the evaluation protocol; first paper on per-well coverage failure and remedies.
Year 2: decision-aware calibration and structured decoding; second paper; secondment or collaboration with an industrial partner where possible.
Year 3: extension to prognostics and digital twins; third paper; thesis writing and open-source release.

6. Expected outcomes and impact
Three peer-reviewed papers, an open benchmark protocol and software toolkit, and guidance for deploying trustworthy ML in safety-critical industrial settings. Negative results will be reported openly.

7. Ethics, data and intellectual property
Only public data will be used unless an agreement is in place. Technical details of my existing patent applications are confidential and will not be disclosed or used without separate agreement.

8. Why me
MSc in Petroleum Engineering (Drilling) and several years of industrial and product-development experience, including digital-twin and predictive-maintenance work for gas compressors and turbines. English proficiency: C2.

Preliminary, unpublished experiments on public data illustrate the problem. In a well-log facies study on the FORCE 2020 data (81 wells), split conformal prediction reached an average coverage of 0.889 against a 0.90 target, but the worst well reached only 0.599 and 19 of 81 wells fell below 0.85. Aim: to develop and rigorously evaluate uncertainty-quantification methods whose guarantees hold per well, per asset and under distribution shift, and that connect directly to operational decisions.

RQ3. Can domain structure (stratigraphic transition grammars, drilling mechanics, physics-based digital twins) improve validity and sample efficiency without sacrificing coverage?

Title

Machine-learning models are increasingly used to support high-stakes engineering decisions: interpreting well logs while drilling, detecting abnormal operating states and scheduling maintenance of gas compressors and turbines. In these settings the cost of an unreliable prediction is large, yet the standard evaluation (random train/test splits and average accuracy) hides the failure that matters: a model that is well calibrated on average can be badly miscalibrated on a particular well, machine or operating regime. My professional work as a petroleum (drilling) engineer and as the developer of AI products for oil and gas, health and other industrial domains has repeatedly shown this gap between benchmark performance and decision-ready reliability.

Preliminary, unpublished experiments on public data illustrate the problem. In a well-log facies study on the FORCE 2020 data (81 wells), split conformal prediction reached an average coverage of 0.889 against a 0.90 target, but the worst well reached only 0.599 and 19 of 81 wells fell below 0.85. In an alarm-design study on real Petrobras 3W instances (1,119 events) the false-alarm rate was 0.147 against a target of 0.10. These are early results from prototypes, not validated findings; they motivate the question below.

Aim: to develop and rigorously evaluate uncertainty-quantification methods whose guarantees hold per well, per asset and under distribution shift, and that connect directly to operational decisions.
RQ1. How can group-conditional and adaptive conformal prediction, and Bayesian ensembles, be made reliable at the level of individual wells or machines when the test distribution differs from the training data?
RQ2. How should calibrated uncertainty be coupled to cost-sensitive decisions (alarm, referral to an expert, intervention) so that operational costs, not only accuracy, are minimised?
RQ3. Can domain structure (stratigraphic transition grammars, drilling mechanics, physics-based digital twins) improve validity and sample efficiency without sacrificing coverage?

Three peer-reviewed papers, an open benchmark protocol and software toolkit, and guidance for deploying trustworthy ML in safety-critical industrial settings. Negative results will be reported openly.

Only public data will be used unless an agreement is in place. Technical details of my existing patent applications are confidential and will not be disclosed or used without separate agreement.

Status note: this programme's details and deadline are recorded as unconfirmed in the dashboard; check the official page before use.

Title
Decision-making under AI uncertainty in industrial operations: how calibrated uncertainty reporting changes maintenance and drilling decisions

1. Background and motivation
Organisations in energy and heavy industry increasingly rely on machine-learning predictions for operational decisions such as scheduling maintenance, raising alarms or interpreting well data. Managers usually see a single score, not how reliable it is for the machine or well in front of them. A model that is well calibrated on average can be unreliable in a specific regime, so decisions made on it carry hidden risk. Little management research examines how the way uncertainty is reported shapes decisions and outcomes in these settings.

2. Research questions
RQ1. How do decision-makers in industrial operations interpret and use AI predictions with and without calibrated uncertainty information?
RQ2. Which organisational conditions (roles, incentives, accountability and trust) determine whether uncertainty information is acted upon?
RQ3. What is the economic value of calibrated, decision-aware reporting compared with point predictions, for maintenance and operations choices?

3. Design and methods
(a) Quantitative: simulation of operational decisions on public industrial datasets (for example well logs and equipment degradation data) comparing decision cost with and without calibrated uncertainty.
(b) Behavioural: a decision experiment with practitioners using the same cases.
(c) Qualitative: interviews and case studies with engineering and management staff to understand adoption barriers.
All data will be public or anonymised; ethical approval will be sought before any human-subject work.

4. Preliminary evidence
In unpublished public-data experiments (81 wells, FORCE 2020), split conformal prediction reached an average coverage of 0.889 against a 0.90 target, but the worst well reached only 0.599. This shows that average reliability hides well-specific failures, which is the managerial problem above. These are early prototype results, not validated findings.

5. Expected contribution
A theory-informed account of how uncertainty reporting affects operational decisions, an empirically grounded cost model, and practical guidance for organisations adopting AI in safety-critical operations.

6. Timeline (3–4 years)
Year 1: literature review, framework and pilot study. Year 2: simulation and behavioural experiment. Year 3: case studies and analysis. Year 4: writing, dissemination and thesis.

7. Why me
MSc in Petroleum Engineering (Drilling); founding and leadership experience in technology start-ups and product development for oil and gas, health and other industrial domains; practical familiarity with industrial data and with commercialising technology. English proficiency C2.

Prepared for: University of Erfurt doctoral position

Fit: the field has limited overlap with AI and engineering according to the dashboard; adapt only if a supervisor in a related area is confirmed.

Title
Calibrated, decision-aware uncertainty for machine learning in drilling and industrial asset monitoring under distribution shift

1. Background and motivation
Machine-learning models are increasingly used to support high-stakes engineering decisions: interpreting well logs while drilling, detecting abnormal operating states and scheduling maintenance of gas compressors and turbines. In these settings the cost of an unreliable prediction is large, yet the standard evaluation (random train/test splits and average accuracy) hides the failure that matters: a model that is well calibrated on average can be badly miscalibrated on a particular well, machine or operating regime. My professional work as a petroleum (drilling) engineer and as the developer of AI products for oil and gas, health and other industrial domains has repeatedly shown this gap between benchmark performance and decision-ready reliability.

Preliminary, unpublished experiments on public data illustrate the problem. In a well-log facies study on the FORCE 2020 data (81 wells), split conformal prediction reached an average coverage of 0.889 against a 0.90 target, but the worst well reached only 0.599 and 19 of 81 wells fell below 0.85. In an alarm-design study on real Petrobras 3W instances (1,119 events) the false-alarm rate was 0.147 against a target of 0.10. These are early results from prototypes, not validated findings; they motivate the question below.

2. Aims and research questions
Aim: to develop and rigorously evaluate uncertainty-quantification methods whose guarantees hold per well, per asset and under distribution shift, and that connect directly to operational decisions.
RQ1. How can group-conditional and adaptive conformal prediction, and Bayesian ensembles, be made reliable at the level of individual wells or machines when the test distribution differs from the training data?
RQ2. How should calibrated uncertainty be coupled to cost-sensitive decisions (alarm, referral to an expert, intervention) so that operational costs, not only accuracy, are minimised?
RQ3. Can domain structure (stratigraphic transition grammars, drilling mechanics, physics-based digital twins) improve validity and sample efficiency without sacrificing coverage?

3. Literature and positioning
The work builds on conformal prediction and its group-conditional, adaptive and shift-aware extensions, on Bayesian deep learning and deep ensembles, on cost-sensitive decision theory, and on physics-informed and structured prediction in geoscience and prognostics. The gap I address is empirical and methodological: few studies evaluate guarantees on a leave-one-well-out or leave-one-asset-out basis with real industrial benchmarks, and fewer connect the guarantees to decision costs. A full literature review will be completed in the first year.

4. Methodology
(a) Evaluation protocol: leave-one-well-out and leave-one-asset-out splits, worst-group coverage and decision-cost metrics reported alongside averages. (b) Methods: group-conditional and adaptive conformal prediction, Bayesian deep ensembles, structured decoding with domain grammars, and cost-sensitive referral policies; reinforcement learning for sequential decisions will be considered where a simulator exists. (c) Data: public datasets only (FORCE 2020 and SEG 2016 well logs, Petrobras 3W v2, NASA IMS bearings, further sets identified in year one), with licences verified before use; industrial data would be used only under a confidentiality agreement. (d) Software: an open-source, tested and reproducible toolkit.

5. Work plan (three years)
Year 1: literature review; reproducible baselines and the evaluation protocol; first paper on per-well coverage failure and remedies.
Year 2: decision-aware calibration and structured decoding; second paper; secondment or collaboration with an industrial partner where possible.
Year 3: extension to prognostics and digital twins; third paper; thesis writing and open-source release.

6. Expected outcomes and impact
Three peer-reviewed papers, an open benchmark protocol and software toolkit, and guidance for deploying trustworthy ML in safety-critical industrial settings. Negative results will be reported openly.

7. Ethics, data and intellectual property
Only public data will be used unless an agreement is in place. Technical details of my existing patent applications are confidential and will not be disclosed or used without separate agreement.

8. Why me
MSc in Petroleum Engineering (Drilling) and several years of industrial and product-development experience, including digital-twin and predictive-maintenance work for gas compressors and turbines. English proficiency: C2.
